title: Prošlost
theme: Past tense uses sam plus -o, -la, or -lo, so gender shows up on the doing-word.

whyHere.heading: Why you are here
whyHere.body: Today you learn how Bosnian builds the past with a little helper plus a gendered piece of the doing-word. English says I worked and she worked with the same worked. Bosnian says Radio sam if Emir worked and Radila sam if Ana worked. The helper is sam, si, or je for one person, and the other piece takes -o, -la, or -lo to match who did it. This chapter is only that past.

englishLies.heading: Why English lies
englishLies.body: English lies because the past ending on the doing-word usually ignores whether the speaker is a man or a woman. I cooked and she cooked share cooked. Bosnian hangs gender on the past form itself. Bio is he was. Bila is she was. Bilo is leftover was. Schools call the helper forms of biti, and they call the whole tense prošlost, which means the past. You can keep saying sam plus the gendered piece and still be right.

knownLine.heading: A line you already say
knownLine.body: Book 1 already taught you Ana, Emir, and the short word sam in lines like Ovdje sam. Today that helper joins the past. Emir can say Bio sam u Sarajevu, which means I was in Sarajevo. Ana can say Bila sam na moru, which means I was at the sea. Same helper family. Different gendered piece because Emir is he and Ana is she. The coffee and the house stay in their Chapter 1 piles. The new work is on the doing-word.
knownLine.speaker: Emir

pattern.heading: The pattern
pattern.body: Build the everyday past in two parts. First pick the helper that matches who. Ja takes sam, ti takes si, and on or ona takes je. Then pick the gendered piece of the verb. He-pile who gets -o, as in bio, radio, and pio. She-pile who gets -la, as in bila, radila, and pila. Leftover who gets -lo, as in bilo when pivo or Sarajevo is the subject. The helper can sit in second place, so Bio sam and Ja sam bio both appear. Learn Emir versus Ana first. Then notice leftover ono uses -lo.

howYouGuess.heading: The pests
howYouGuess.body: Two pests will trip you today. The first pest is matching the past ending to the thing you drank instead of the person who drank. Ana says Pila sam kahvu with -la because Ana is she, not because coffee somehow became she in the past. The second pest is forgetting the helper. Radio without sam is not a finished everyday past for I worked. Keep sam, si, or je in the sentence. Those two habits will save you more grief than any new chart.

trick.heading: The bit that tricks you
trick.body: The trap is to hear -la and decide the whole sentence flipped into the she pile for every noun. The -la marks who did the action, usually the person. Kahvu can still sit in its want-it form beside that past. The other trap is to copy English and put a he ending on a she speaker. If Ana did it, use radila. If Emir did it, use radio. Leftover subjects take -lo, and that form shows up less in café talk, so master he and she first.

nerd.heading: Why it's like this
nerd.body:
Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. It had richer past forms than yours, but it did not keep a clean he-worked versus she-worked split on the verb the way Bosnian does. Later English locked past on time words and endings like -ed. You speak that later version.

Bosnian past is an old combo. A short piece of to be plus an old verbal adjective that still agrees in gender. That is why Ana and Emir diverge on radila versus radio even when English keeps worked still. Schools may say L-participle once. You only need sam plus the gendered piece. Tomorrow adds the future helper and the everyday can-must-want row.

items.prompt: Ana. I was at the sea.

items.explanation: Helper je with bila for ona.

items.prompt: Why does Ana say Pila sam kahvu with -la?
items.explanation: The gendered piece matches who did it.

items.prompt: What is missing in Radio without a helper for I worked?
items.explanation: Everyday past wants sam, si, or je.

items.prompt: Emir went to the bridge. Which form?
items.explanation: Išao is the he past of ići.
Pivo is leftover. The past piece follows the subject pile.

questions.question: Emir. Which past line also parks sam correctly after Ja?
questions.explanation: Bio sam and Ja sam bio both work. Sam stays in second place. Sam bio cannot open the line.

questions.question: Why is Ana je bila ovdje right?
options: Because je matches ona and bila matches Ana
questions.explanation: Helper je plus she piece bila.

questions.question: The -la in Pila sam kahvu matches which who?
questions.explanation: Gender on the past piece follows who did the action.

questions.question: What comes next?
options: Clitic second place as the only topic
questions.explanation: Chapter 11 bundles the future helper, commands, and everyday modals.

next.body: You now can build Bio sam and Bila sam, and you know the -la follows Ana, not the coffee. Chapter 11 adds the future with ću, blunt versus polite commands, and the everyday row for can, must, and want. You still only own the past from today.
